summary.text: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the historical northern borders of Chinese states as protection against nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe.
The first walls date to the 7th century BC and were joined together in the Qin dynasty, and successive dynasties expanded the system.
The best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty, and the whole system spans 21,196.18 km (13,170.70 mi) in total.

facts.value: Built by the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644)

items.prompt: After unification, Qin's ruler tore down the walls that divided the former states. Why did he still order new wall-building in the north?

options.label: To mark a permanent border that would never move
To connect the remaining northern fortifications against the Xiongnu
To keep former feudal lords apart from each other
To collect duties on goods moving along the Silk Road

items.explain: To position the empire against the Xiongnu, he ordered new walls connecting the remaining fortifications along the northern frontier, and it was not meant as a permanently fixed border.

items.prompt: A work crew must build a wall segment across a flat plain far from any stone. Following the builders' approach, which material fits?

options.label: Hauled-in stone
Fired brick
Imported timber
Rammed earth

items.explain: Builders used local resources: stone in montane areas and rammed earth in the plains.

items.prompt: After a defeat by the Oirats at the Battle of Tumu, amid long conflict with Mongol tribes, how did the Ming change their defense?

options.label: They built walls along the northern border
They abandoned the north and moved the capital
They tore down older walls to trade freely
They relied on watchtowers in the south alone

items.explain: A new strategy for defense was realized by constructing walls along the northern border of China.

items.prompt: Why was Ming construction stronger and more elaborate than earlier fortifications?

options.label: Builders packed earth and gravel between board frames
Builders used timber for the whole structure
Builders used bricks and stone instead of rammed earth
Builders relied on local mud alone

items.explain: Earlier walls were mostly stone or stamped earth and gravel between board frames, whereas the Ming used bricks and stone instead of rammed earth.

items.prompt: Why did dynasties after Qin usually avoid calling their own additions the 'Long Wall'?

options.label: The name was tied to the First Emperor's supposed tyranny
The name was reserved for walls made of stone
European travelers had already named it differently
The name meant a city rampart, not a border

items.explain: Because of the wall's association with the First Emperor's supposed tyranny, later dynasties usually avoided the name Long Wall for their own additions.

paragraphs.heading: What the wall is
paragraphs.text: The Great Wall of China is really a whole series of forts and walls. They were built along the old northern borders of Chinese states to guard against nomadic peoples from the Eurasian Steppe. Taken together they reach from Liaodong in the east all the way west to Lop Lake, in an arc that roughly traces the edge of the Mongolian steppe, and they add up to 21,196.18 km (13,170.70 mi). Today the wall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a 2007 vote named it among the New 7 Wonders of the World.

paragraphs.heading: More than a barrier
paragraphs.text: The wall defended with watchtowers, barracks for troops and garrison stations. Signals could be sent along it with smoke or fire, and it also served as a corridor for transport. It controlled who came in and went out, it allowed duties to be charged on goods carried along the Silk Road, and it helped regulate trade.

paragraphs.heading: Walls between rival states
paragraphs.text: The first walls date to the 7th century BC. Chinese builders already knew how to make walls in the Spring and Autumn period, which ran from the 8th to the 5th century BC. In that era and the Warring States period after it, many states, among them Qin, Chu, Zhao, Qi and Yan, built long fortifications around their own borders. Meant to resist swords and spears, they were mostly made of stone, or of earth and gravel pounded between wooden board frames.

paragraphs.heading: The Qin join them up
paragraphs.text: When the state of Qin won in 221 BC, its ruler became the First Emperor of a united China. He tore down the walls that split his empire along the old state lines, but ordered new ones to link up the walls on the northern frontier against the Xiongnu. A guiding rule was build and move on, so this was not meant as a fixed, permanent border. Builders used what was nearby, stone in the mountains and rammed earth on the plains. Most Qin walls have worn away, and no records give their exact length or route.

paragraphs.heading: Later dynasties
paragraphs.text: Later, the Han, the Sui and the Northern dynasties spent heavily to repair, rebuild or extend parts of the wall. The Tang and Song did little in the region. Dynasties founded by non-Han peoples, such as the Northern Wei, the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia, also built defensive walls, but farther north, reaching toward present-day Mongolia.

paragraphs.heading: The Ming wall
paragraphs.text: The best-known sections come from the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). After losing to the Oirats at the Battle of Tumu, during a long struggle with Mongol tribes, the Ming chose a new defence plan of walls along the northern border. They built with brick and stone rather than rammed earth, so their wall was stronger and more elaborate than earlier ones. As many as 25,000 watchtowers may have stood on it, and the stretches near the capital, Beijing, were especially strong. Between 1567 and 1570, under general Qi Jiguang, 1,200 watchtowers went up between Shanhaiguan Pass and Changping.

paragraphs.heading: What's in a name
paragraphs.text: In Chinese the wall is called Chángchéng, the Long Wall, a term found in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. The longer name, Ten-Thousand-Mile-Long Wall, uses ten thousand to mean countless, not as an exact count. Because the Long Wall was tied to the First Emperor's supposed tyranny, later dynasties mostly avoided that name for their own additions. Only under the Qing did it become the general word for all the border walls. The English name grew out of European travellers' talk of the Chinese wall, and by the nineteenth century the Great Wall of China was standard.
